newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia's Lebed says U.S. "spitting on everybody".
newsitem.headline: Russia's Lebed says U.S. "spitting on everybody".

text.p: Russian security chief Alexander Lebed said on Thursday the United States was behaving like a "bull in a china shop" with its air strikes against Iraq, amid conflicting reports about whether Moscow had been warned in advance.
"There is one big strong master (in the world) who spits on everybody," Interfax news agency quoted Lebed as saying.
"That master is behaving like a bull in a china shop," it said Lebed had told journalists during his latest peace mission to the rebel Russian region of Chechnya.
With characteristic cynicism, the growling former paratroop general went on to say that U.S. President Bill Clinton had carried out the attacks to boost his democratic image.
"This is the essence of true democracy -- carry out air raids and then gather the journalists to applaud," Lebed said.

Lebed's salvo was the latest of a series of Russian denunciations of the air strikes, launched by Washington against Iraq on Tuesday and Wednesday in retaliation for Baghdad's military operation against separatist Kurds in the north.
On Thursday President Boris Yeltsin's foreign affairs adviser Dmitry Ryurikov told a news briefing Russia's leadership had not been not informed of the U.S. plans in advance.
"To talk about coordination is simply not serious...The Russian leadership was not informed," Ryurikov said.
Yeltsin's chief of staff Anatoly Chubais had earlier indicated that Russia had been consulted on Monday, the day before the first wave of strikes.
"To raise the question that such a scale of events could have occurred without consultations with Russia is simply irresponsible," Chubais said on Wednesday.
Deputy Foreign Minister Viktor Posuvalyuk came up with yet another version of events surrounding the U.S. strikes.

"The Russian Federation and the U.S. were in constant contact with one another and the Americans spoke repeatedly about their readiness to take the most diverse measures to alter the situation in northern Iraq," Interfax quoted him as saying.

"We underlined every time that we are categorically opposed to the use of force against Baghdad," he said, adding that judging by Clinton's remark that the attacks had achieved their goal, he did not expect further strikes.

Russia has generally taken a softer line on Iraq than the United States since the end of the Gulf conflict, and has been pushing Washington and its Western European allies to lift crippling post-war sanctions against Baghdad.

Moscow fears the latest crisis could hurt its chances of recouping Baghdad's massive debt to the former Soviet Union because it has delayed a United Nations agreement to let sanction-squeezed Iraq sell some oil.

Ryurikov said the events in Iraq would be discussed during talks planned for Saturday near Moscow between Yeltsin and German Chancellor Helmut Kohl, although he said Kohl's visit had been arranged before the latest crisis.

Deputy Foreign Minister Vasily Sidorov said Moscow would also veto a British draft resolution condemning Iraq for its offensive in the north if it was offered to the United Nations Security Concil unchanged.

The draft, which condemns Iraq's operations in the northern city of Arbit and "expresses grave concern" about a wider escalation of hostilities in the region, demands Iraqi troops withdraw immediately.
It makes no mention of the U.S. missile attacks.

Russia's ambassador to the United Nations, Sergei Lavrov, had insisted that Baghdad's troops entered their own territory at the request of one Kurdish party and hinted Moscow might abstain if no compromise was found before the draft is put to a vote.
